name: Metraleeswarar Temple, Kanchipuram
deity: Shiva as Metraleeswarar (Metralinathar), with the goddess Metralanayagi
period: Ancient Shiva shrine of Kanchipuram sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with later additions
dynasty: Medieval Tamil patrons (Pallava and later Chola era)
summary: Metraleeswarar, the Thirumetrali of the Tevaram hymns, is one of the ancient Shiva temples within the temple-city of Kanchipuram, remembered for a sanctum that faces west — for, by tradition, the Lord turned toward the west to hear the hymns of the child-saint Sambandar.

sections.history: Kanchipuram, one of the seven sacred cities of the Hindu tradition and long a capital of the Tamil country, holds a great company of ancient shrines, and Metraleeswarar is among those sung by the Tevaram saints and so counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam. In the hymns the shrine is called Thirumetrali. Tradition explains the name from the direction the Lord faces: as Shiva is said to have turned to the west — merku in Tamil — to listen to the songs of the child-saint Sambandar, the place became Thirumetrali and the deity Metralinathar, the Lord of the western shrine. The temple stands in the Pillayarpalayam quarter of the old city, raised and maintained in stone across the centuries and kept in worship to this day under the state endowments board.
sections.architecture: Unusually among Shiva temples, the sanctum of Metraleeswarar faces west, holding the Lord in the form of a granite linga. The eastern gateway rises as a three-tiered rajagopuram. Within the enclosure the goddess, honoured here as Metralanayagi, is given her own shrine — a notable feature in Kanchipuram, where tradition holds Kamakshi to be the common Mother Goddess of the city's Shiva temples. The walls and niches carry the attendant forms of a Dravidian shrine, and the temple keeps the compact, self-contained plan of the older sanctuaries of the city.
sections.legends: The temple's defining story is woven into its very name. When the child-saint Sambandar came to Kanchi and sang before the Lord, Shiva is said to have turned westward to hear the hymns, and from that turning the shrine took the name Thirumetrali. A second tradition tells of Vishnu, who performed penance here and, melting at the power of the sacred songs, took the form of a linga — remembered in the name Odavurugeeswarar, the Lord who melted and flowed. Such legends bind the shrine to the oldest devotional memory of the Tamil land, with the saints and their hymns at the centre of its sanctity.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the festivals of the Shaiva calendar, with the Gurupuja of Thirugnana Sambandar and Panguni Uthiram in March or April among the most prominent. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. The dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: A visit to Metraleeswarar is a quiet one, away from the great crowds that gather at Kanchipuram's largest shrines. Enter beneath the eastern tower, come before the west-facing sanctum of the Lord, and turn to the goddess Metralanayagi in her own shrine. The temple sits within the lanes of the old city, close to other ancient sanctuaries, and rewards the pilgrim who walks Kanchi shrine by shrine.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the Pillayarpalayam area of Kanchipuram, in the north of the old city. Kanchipuram is well connected by rail and road and lies about 75 km from Chennai, whose international airport is the nearest. Local buses and autos reach the quarter, and the temple is a short walk within the lanes.
